level.hints.title: Hints

level.debrief.title: What you just did
level.w1-l3.title: Roll Downhill
level.w1-l3.mission: Get the ball into the valley in 15 steps or fewer. Before each step, choose how far to go.
level.w1-l3.hint1: Watch the hollow ball before you step: it shows where you will land. Is it closer to the valley, or past it?
level.w1-l3.hint2: The arrow always points downhill. Where the ground is steep, a big step overshoots; where it is flat, a small step wastes moves.
level.w1-l3.hint3: Start small, around 0.08, while the slope is steep. Once the ball is in the long valley, raise the step size to about 0.28.
level.w1-l3.debrief: That was gradient descent. Each step moves the model's parameters against the slope of the loss, and your step size is the learning rate. Too small wastes steps, too large overshoots, and the best optimizers adapt the step as the slope changes.
codex.lede: Every level you beat adds the idea you just used, in plain words.
concept.gradient-descent.definition: Improving a model by repeatedly moving its parameters a small step against the slope of the loss. The size of that step is the learning rate.
map.levels.label: Levels in {world}
level.w1-l1.title: Draw the Line
level.w1-l1.mission: These points follow a trend. Drag the two handles so the line runs through the middle of the cloud, then check your line.
level.w1-l1.hint1: The thin vertical lines show how far each point is from your line. Try to make them short everywhere, not just in one place.
level.w1-l1.hint2: A good line has about as many points above it as below it, at both ends of the cloud.
level.w1-l1.hint3: Put the left handle near 6 and the right handle near 18.4, then check.
level.w1-l1.debrief: You just fit a linear model: ŷ = w·x + b. Moving the handles chose the slope w and the intercept b, and the error lines you shrank are the model's mistakes. The third star checked that your line also works on points it never saw.
level.w1-l2.title: Feel the Loss
level.w1-l2.mission: Now every move shows the loss: the average squared error of your line. Make it as low as you can in 20 moves or fewer, then check.
level.w1-l2.hint1: Watch the loss after each move. If it went up, move back the other way.
level.w1-l2.hint2: Errors are squared, so a far-away point counts a lot. Aim through the middle of the whole cloud, not just the nearby points.
level.w1-l2.hint3: Put the left handle near 5.7 and the right handle near 19, then nudge each one until the loss stops dropping.
level.w1-l2.debrief: That number was the loss, here the mean squared error. Training a model means searching for the parameters that make it as small as possible. You searched by hand; in the next levels, gradient descent does the searching for you.
concept.linear-regression.definition: Predicting a number with a straight line, ŷ = w·x + b. Training means choosing the slope w and intercept b that fit the data best.
concept.loss-function.definition: One number that measures how wrong a model is. Mean squared error averages the squared distance between predictions and true values, and training tries to make it small.
level.line.hint: Drag the orange handles, or focus one and use the arrow keys (hold Shift for bigger moves).
level.plot.description: Scatter plot of {count} points with your line. Short vertical lines show each point's error.
level.loss.label: Loss (mean squared error)
level.result.fit.passed.title: Good fit
level.result.fit.failed.title: Not a good fit yet
level.result.fit.passed.body: Your line's mean squared error is {loss}.
level.result.fail.final_loss: Your line's mean squared error is {actual}. It needs to be below {expected}.
level.result.fail.loss_gap: Your line's loss is {actual} above the best possible. Get within {expected}.
level.result.fail.moves: You used {actual} moves; the limit is {expected}.
level.result.next.moves: Next star: find it in {value} moves or fewer.
level.result.next.loss_gap: Next star: get within {value} of the lowest possible loss.
level.result.next.test_loss: Next star: a line that also fits points it hasn't seen (hidden loss at most {value}).
level.w1-l4.title: Too Fast, Too Slow
level.w1-l4.mission: This time gradient descent moves the line for you. Choose a learning rate and press Train. The line has to settle on the data within 50 epochs without blowing up.
level.w1-l4.hint1: Try the extremes first: a very small rate, then a very large one. Watch how the loss curve behaves each time.
level.w1-l4.hint2: A curve that falls slowly and smoothly means the rate is too small. A curve that zigzags or climbs means it is too large.
level.w1-l4.hint3: The fastest rates for this data sit between about 0.4 and 0.7.
level.w1-l4.debrief: The learning rate is the size of each gradient-descent step. Too small and training crawls; too large and every step overshoots, until the loss bounces or explodes. In between is a sweet spot that converges in a handful of epochs, and finding it is one of the first things you tune on any real model.
concept.learning-rate.definition: How far each gradient-descent step moves the parameters. Too small trains slowly; too large overshoots and can make training diverge.
level.learningRate.label: Learning rate
level.learningRate.hint: How big a step gradient descent takes each epoch. Pick one, then press Train.
level.curve.description: Loss curve over {epochs} epochs of training, on a logarithmic scale.
level.curve.empty: Press Train to see the loss curve.
level.result.train.converged.title: Converged
level.result.train.converged.body: With learning rate {rate}, training converged in {epochs, plural, one {# epoch} other {# epochs}}.
level.result.train.slow.title: Too slow
level.result.train.slow.body: With learning rate {rate}, the loss is still {gap} above the best possible after {epochs} epochs. Try a larger learning rate.
level.result.train.diverged.title: Too fast: the loss blew up
level.result.train.diverged.body: With learning rate {rate}, every step overshot the minimum by more than the last, so the loss exploded. Try a smaller learning rate.
level.result.next.epochs_to_converge: Next star: converge in {value} epochs or fewer.
level.w1-l5.title: Bumpy Terrain
level.w1-l5.mission: This landscape has several valleys, and only one is the deepest. Choose where the ball starts, then roll it. Gradient descent will carry it downhill into whichever valley it starts above.
level.w1-l5.hint1: The ball can only feel the slope right under it. It will stop at the bottom of the first valley it rolls into, deep or not.
level.w1-l5.hint2: Look for the valley with the most rings around it: more rings means deeper. Then find the high ground that drains into it.
level.w1-l5.hint3: The deepest valley is on the right, a little below the middle. Start anywhere on the right third of the map.
level.w1-l5.debrief: The ball stopped in a local minimum whenever it started in the wrong valley: gradient descent only follows the slope under it, so where you start decides where you end up. Real training has the same problem, which is why starting points, randomness and restarts matter.
concept.local-minimum.definition: A point where the loss is lower than everything nearby but not the lowest overall. Gradient descent can get stuck there, because every direction around it goes uphill.
level.start.hint: Click or tap the map to place the ball, or focus the map and use the arrow keys. Then roll it.
level.start.label: Starting point. Use the arrow keys to move it.
level.result.valley.passed.title: Deepest valley
level.result.valley.passed.body: The ball settled on the valley floor in {steps, plural, one {# step} other {# steps}}.
level.result.valley.local.title: Stuck in a local minimum
level.result.valley.local.body: The ball settled in a valley, but not the deepest one: it ended {distance} away from the lowest point. Pick a start that drains into the deepest valley.
level.result.next.attempt: Next star: get it on your first roll.
level.result.next.epochs_to_converge.lan: Next star: settle in {value} steps or fewer, by starting closer.
level.w1-l6.title: Dirty Data
level.w1-l6.mission: Some of these measurements are broken, and they drag the best-fit line off the trend. Remove the bad points, then check the line against fresh data it has never seen.
level.w1-l6.hint1: Watch the line as you remove a point. A bad point makes the line jump; a normal point barely moves it.
level.w1-l6.hint2: The long error lines point at the suspects: points far from where the rest of the cloud says they should be.
level.w1-l6.hint3: There are four broken points, all at the right end and far below the others.
level.w1-l6.debrief: Those points were outliers: bad measurements far from the pattern. Mean squared error squares every error, so a few far-away points can pull the whole line off. Cleaning them fixed the model on new data, and keeping the good points kept it honest; deleting real data just because it doesn't fit is its own mistake.
concept.outlier.definition: A data point far from the pattern of the rest, often from a measurement error. Squared-error models are very sensitive to outliers, so they are worth finding before training.
level.cleaning.hint: Click or tap a point to remove it; click it again to put it back. Keyboard: Tab to a point, then press Enter or Space.
level.cleaning.plot: Scatter plot of {count} points with the best-fit line through the ones you kept. Removed points are drawn hollow.
level.result.clean.passed.title: Clean fit
level.result.clean.passed.body: On fresh data your line's error is {loss}. You removed {removed} points.
level.result.clean.failed.title: The fit is still off
level.result.clean.failed.body: On fresh data your line's error is {loss}; it needs to be at most {target}. Something is still pulling the line away from the trend.
level.result.next.good_points_removed: Next star: remove only broken points (you removed {actual} good ones).
level.w1-l7.title: Scale Matters
level.w1-l7.mission: This model has two features, and one is ten times bigger than the other. Train it at least 3 times faster than the best anyone can manage without scaling.
level.w1-l7.hint1: First press Train as it is. That run is about as fast as it gets without scaling: any bigger learning rate blows up.
level.w1-l7.hint2: The big feature makes the loss valley long and narrow, so the learning rate has to stay tiny. Scaling makes both features the same size, and the valley becomes round.
level.w1-l7.hint3: Turn on scaling, then raise the learning rate to around 0.3 to 0.6.
level.w1-l7.debrief: Feature scaling puts every feature on the same footing: minus its mean, divided by its spread. Unscaled, one big feature forces a tiny learning rate, and training crawls along a long, narrow valley. Scaled, the valley is round, a much larger learning rate is safe, and training converges in a few epochs. Scale your features before gradient descent.
concept.feature-scaling.definition: Rescaling each input feature to a similar range, usually by subtracting its mean and dividing by its standard deviation. It lets gradient descent use a larger learning rate and converge much faster.
level.scaling.toggle.hint: Standardize each feature: subtract its mean, divide by its spread.
level.result.scaling.passed.title: {speedup}× faster
level.result.scaling.passed.body: Converged in {epochs, plural, one {# epoch} other {# epochs}}, against {baseline} for the best unscaled run.
level.result.scaling.slow.title: Only {speedup}× faster
level.result.scaling.slow.body: Converged in {epochs, plural, one {# epoch} other {# epochs}}; the best unscaled run needs {baseline}. You need at least 3× faster.
level.result.scaling.unconverged.title: Did not converge
level.result.scaling.unconverged.body: The loss never reached the target within {max} epochs.
level.result.scaling.diverged.title: Too fast: the loss blew up
level.result.scaling.diverged.body: With learning rate {rate}{scaled} every step overshot, so the loss exploded. Try a smaller rate.
level.w1-l8.title: Boss: The Deep Valley
level.w1-l8.mission: Everything from World 1 at once: noisy data with broken points, a feature on a large scale, and a tight budget. Train a line that fits fresh data, converging within 30 epochs.
level.w1-l8.hint1: Three things are wrong here. Press Train once as it is, then read what went wrong.
level.w1-l8.hint2: The large x values make the loss valley so narrow that every learning rate on the slider blows up. And a few points far below the others pull the line down.
level.w1-l8.hint3: Remove the four low points at the right end, turn on scaling, and use a learning rate near 0.5.
level.w1-l8.debrief: That is the everyday recipe for training a model: clean the data, scale the features, then tune the learning rate. Skip any one of them and training blows up, crawls, or learns the wrong thing. World 1, the Valley of Loss, is complete.
concept.preprocessing.definition: Preparing data before training: removing broken points, scaling features to similar ranges, and so on. Good preprocessing is often what makes gradient descent work at all.
level.training.scale.hint: Standardize x before training: subtract its mean, divide by its spread.
level.training.cleaning: Click or tap a point to remove it before training; click again to put it back.
level.result.train.overbudget.title: Converged, but too slowly
level.result.train.overbudget.body: With learning rate {rate}, training took {epochs, plural, one {# epoch} other {# epochs}}; the budget is {limit}.
level.result.train.misfit.title: Trained, but on broken data
level.result.train.misfit.body: Training converged, but the line also fits the broken points: its error on fresh data is {test}, and it needs to be at most {target}.
level.w2-l1.title: Split the Kingdom
level.w2-l1.mission: Two kingdoms share this plain. Drag the two handles to draw a straight border, so each kingdom's people end up on its own side. At least 90% must be on the right side.
level.w2-l1.hint1: The shading shows each kingdom's side. If most people sit in the wrong colour, press Swap sides.
level.w2-l1.hint2: The two groups lean: one sits lower left, the other upper right. A border that follows that lean works best.
level.w2-l1.hint3: Put one handle near the top left corner and the other near the bottom right corner, through the gap between the groups.
level.w2-l1.debrief: You just built a classifier. A straight border, w₁x₁ + w₂x₂ + b = 0, splits the plane into two classes: that is the decision boundary of a linear model like logistic regression. Notice that the border with the most training points right is not always the one that works best on new points.
concept.classification.definition: Predicting a category instead of a number. A linear classifier draws a straight decision boundary and labels each point by which side it falls on.
level.boundary.hint: Drag the orange handles to move the border, or focus a handle and use the arrow keys (Shift for bigger moves).
level.boundary.plot: Map of {count} people from two kingdoms, circles and squares, with your border and each side shaded by kingdom.
level.result.boundary.passed.title: Kingdom split
level.result.boundary.passed.body: {accuracy}% of the people are on the right side of your border.
level.result.boundary.failed.title: Too many on the wrong side
level.result.boundary.failed.body: Only {accuracy}% are on the right side; you need at least {target}%.
level.result.next.accuracy: Next star: get at least {value} right.
level.result.next.test_accuracy: Next star: a border that also works for people it hasn't seen (at least {value} of them right).
level.w2-l2.title: Confidence
level.w2-l2.mission: This model gives each point a probability of being a circle. Move the threshold and the slope until every point gets at least 80% for its own kind, then check. Be confident, but not blindly so.
level.w2-l2.hint1: The threshold is where the curve crosses 50%. Put it in the empty gap between the squares and the circles.
level.w2-l2.hint2: A steeper slope makes the model more certain. Too gentle and nobody reaches 80%; too steep and new points near the border get confidently wrong answers.
level.w2-l2.debrief: That S-shaped curve is the sigmoid: it turns a score into a probability. Logistic regression outputs these probabilities, not just a yes or no. The threshold decides the class; the slope decides how sure it is. A model that is certain about everything pays heavily, in log loss, for every mistake on new data.
concept.sigmoid.definition: The sigmoid squashes any score into a probability between 0 and 1. A classifier's confidence should match reality: too timid is unhelpful, too certain is punished by log loss when it is wrong.
level.sigmoid.slope.hint: How quickly the model switches from square to circle: steeper = more certain.
level.sigmoid.weakest: Least confident point: {confidence}% for its own kind
level.sigmoid.plot: Probability curve from 0 to 1 over {count} points; squares belong at 0, circles at 1. Dashed lines mark 80% confidence.
level.result.sigmoid.passed.title: Confident
level.result.sigmoid.passed.body: Every point gets at least {confidence}% for its own kind.
level.result.sigmoid.failed.title: Not sure enough
level.result.sigmoid.failed.body: The least confident point only gets {confidence}% for its own kind; every point needs at least 80%.
level.result.next.min_confidence: Next star: at least {value} for every point.
level.result.next.test_loss.sigmoid: Next star: less overconfident. New points near the border are being called with too much certainty.
level.w2-l3.title: Not a Straight Line
level.w2-l3.mission: The circle kingdom sits in the middle, surrounded by the square kingdom. No straight border can split them. Choose which features the model sees, train it, and get at least 95% right.
level.w2-l3.hint1: Train with x₁ and x₂ first. A model that only sees x₁ and x₂ can only ever draw a straight border.
level.w2-l3.hint2: Distance from the centre separates the kingdoms. Which features grow with distance from the centre, whatever the direction?
level.w2-l3.hint3: x₁² + x₂² is the squared distance from the centre. Give the model exactly those two features.
level.w2-l3.debrief: The model is still linear, but in new features. On x₁² and x₂², a straight border becomes a circle on the map. That is feature engineering: reshaping the inputs so a simple model can capture a curved pattern. Adding every feature you can think of fits the training points too, but it starts to slip on new ones.
concept.feature-engineering.definition: Creating new inputs from the raw ones, like x₁² or x₁·x₂, so that a simple model can capture curved patterns. The right features matter more than the most features.
level.features.count: {count, plural, one {# feature} other {# features}} selected
level.features.none: Train to see the border this model draws.
level.features.plot: Map of {count} people from two kingdoms, with the regions the trained model assigns to each.
level.result.features.passed.title: Split
level.result.features.passed.body: {accuracy}% right, using {count, plural, one {# feature} other {# features}}.
level.result.features.failed.title: Still not split
level.result.features.failed.body: Only {accuracy}% right; you need at least 95%. With these features the model can't draw the border this map needs.
level.result.next.feature_count: Next star: do it with only {value} features.
level.w2-l4.title: The Overfitter
level.w2-l4.mission: Only twenty people have been surveyed. Choose how flexible the border may be, train to see it, then check it on the rest of the kingdom: it must get at least 85% of new people right.
level.w2-l4.hint1: Train at the highest complexity and look at the border. Does it look like the real divide between two groups, or like it is chasing single points?
level.w2-l4.hint2: With so few points, a flexible model can bend around every one of them, noise included. The training score says nothing about new people.
level.w2-l4.hint3: Complexity 1, a straight border, generalizes best on this data.
level.w2-l4.debrief: That was overfitting: the complex model memorized twenty noisy points, got 100% of them right, and did worse on everyone else. With little data, the simplest model that fits is usually the best. Training accuracy measures memory; only new data measures learning.
concept.overfitting.definition: When a model learns the noise in its training data instead of the pattern, so it scores well on training data and badly on new data. Too much flexibility with too little data is the classic cause.
level.complexity.degree.hint: 1 = straight border. Each step adds terms like x₁², x₁²·x₂, … so the border can bend more.
level.complexity.terms: {count, plural, one {# input} other {# inputs}} to the model
level.complexity.none: Train to see the border at this complexity.
level.result.complexity.passed.title: It generalizes
level.result.complexity.failed.title: Overfitted
level.result.complexity.failed.body: {train}% on the training points, but only {test}% of new people; you need at least 85%.
level.result.next.attempt.overfitter: Next star: get it on your first check.
level.features.plot.checked: Map of {count} people from two kingdoms and {total} new people checked against the trained model; {wrong} of the new people are on the wrong side.
level.complexity.checked: Hollow marks are the {total} new people. The {wrong} crossed out landed on the wrong side of your border.
level.w2-l5.title: Tame It
level.w2-l5.mission: This model has 27 inputs and loves to memorize: it scores far better on the people it was trained on than on anyone new. Turn up the regularization until both scores agree, within 5 points, while still getting at least 85% of new people right.
level.w2-l5.hint1: Train at 0 and look at the border: it twists around single training points. That is where the gap comes from.
level.w2-l5.hint2: Regularization makes large weights expensive, so the border has to stay smooth. A little goes a long way; too much and the model can't even fit what it has seen.
level.w2-l5.debrief: That was regularization: instead of taking inputs away, you kept all 27 and charged the model for using big weights. The border smoothed out, the training score dropped a little, and the two scores met. Push too hard and the model underfits: now it's wrong about the training points too. The right strength is found by checking on data the model hasn't seen.
concept.regularization.definition: A penalty on large model weights (L2: strength × the sum of squared weights) added to the loss. It keeps a flexible model smooth, trading a little training accuracy for better accuracy on new data.
level.regularization.label: Regularization strength (λ)
level.regularization.hint: 0 = no penalty. Higher values punish big weights, so the border has to stay smooth.
level.complexity.fixed: Degree {degree}: {count, plural, one {# input} other {# inputs}} to the model
level.result.tame.passed.title: Tamed
level.result.tame.passed.body: Training {train}%, new people {test}%: a gap of {gap} points.
level.result.tame.over.title: Still memorizing
level.result.tame.over.body: Training {train}%, but new people only {test}%: a gap of {gap} points. It needs to be under 5 with at least 85% on new people.
level.result.tame.under.title: Too tame
level.result.tame.under.body: New people {test}%, but training only {train}%: the penalty is so strong the model can't fit what it has seen. A gap of {gap} points; it needs to be under 5.
level.result.next.accuracy_gap: Next star: find the strength where the two scores match exactly.
level.result.next.attempt.within: Next star: get it within {value} checks.
level.w2-l6.title: Unfair Data
level.w2-l6.mission: Only one person in ten comes from the hill clans (the green circles). The census keeps missing them. Train a border that finds at least 80% of the hill folk among new people.
level.w2-l6.hint1: Train at ×1 and count: the model gets almost every lowlander right, and that alone scores about 90%. Missing hill folk costs it almost nothing.
level.w2-l6.hint2: Make each hill-clan point count more, so a miss hurts the model as much as missing many lowlanders.
level.w2-l6.hint3: There are about ten lowlanders for every hill-clan person. Try a weight near ×10.
level.w2-l6.debrief: That was class imbalance: when one class is rare, a model can score high accuracy by mostly ignoring it, so accuracy alone lies. Recall asks the right question: of the people you were meant to find, how many did you find? Copying the rare class (oversampling) or weighting it rebalances the training. Push it too far and you start flagging everyone.
concept.class-imbalance.definition: When one class is much rarer than the other, accuracy hides the misses. Recall (found ÷ all that exist) measures how many of the rare class a model finds. Oversampling or class weights make the rare class count more in training.
level.oversample.label: Weight of each hill-clan point
level.oversample.hint: ×1 = counts like anyone else. At ×10, nine hill folk weigh as much as ninety lowlanders.
level.oversample.trained: Training: found {found} of {minority} hill folk, {right} of {majority} lowlanders right
level.result.minority.passed.title: Hill folk found
level.result.minority.passed.body: Found {recall}% of the new hill folk, with {test}% of everyone right.
level.result.minority.failed.title: Accuracy lied
level.result.minority.failed.body: {test}% of new people right, but it found only {recall}% of the hill folk; you need at least 80%.
level.result.next.test_accuracy.minority: Next star: flag fewer lowlanders by mistake: keep at least {value}% of everyone right.
level.w2-l7.title: Read the Matrix
level.w2-l7.mission: The king invites hill-clan elders to council, but every invitation costs a rider. The model is trained; you choose how sure it must be before it sends one. Among new people, invite at least 75% of the hill folk, and make sure at least 65% of invitations reach hill folk.
level.w2-l7.hint1: The matrix shows the training people: hill folk found or missed, lowlanders invited by mistake or rightly left out. Check starts from the default threshold 0.5. Look at the missed hill folk.
level.w2-l7.hint2: Lowering the threshold sends invitations to people the model is less sure about: more hill folk found (recall up), but more lowlanders invited too (precision down).
level.w2-l7.hint3: Aim for both numbers under the matrix to clear their targets with a little room: around 0.25 to 0.35.
level.w2-l7.debrief: You just traded precision for recall. Recall asks: of the people you should find, how many did you? Precision asks: of the people you picked, how many were right? One threshold moves both in opposite directions, and the confusion matrix shows exactly what each choice costs. Which balance is right depends on what a miss and a false alarm cost.
concept.precision-recall.term: Precision, recall and the confusion matrix
concept.precision-recall.definition: A confusion matrix counts found, missed, false alarms and correct rejections. Recall = found ÷ all real positives; precision = found ÷ all positive calls. Moving the decision threshold trades one for the other.
level.matrix.threshold: Invite when the model is at least this sure
level.matrix.threshold.hint: The probability of being hill folk needed to send an invitation. 0.5 = the default.
level.matrix.caption: The {total} training people at this threshold
level.result.matrix.passed.title: Council called
level.result.matrix.passed.body: Among new people: {recall}% of the hill folk invited (recall), and {precision}% of invitations reached them (precision).
level.result.matrix.recall.title: Elders left out
level.result.matrix.recall.body: Only {recall}% of the new hill folk were invited; you need {target}%. (Precision: {precision}%.)
level.result.matrix.precision.title: Riders wasted
level.result.matrix.precision.body: Only {precision}% of invitations reached hill folk; you need {target}%. (Recall: {recall}%.)
level.w2-l8.title: Boss: Border War
level.w2-l8.mission: Raiders hide among the villages at the heart of the plains: about one person in seven, and the records are noisy. Flag them so the border holds on new people: a hidden F1 score of at least 0.85. Every tool from this world is yours.
level.w2-l8.hint1: A straight border can't enclose the heart of the plains, and flagging nobody scores well on accuracy but F1 0. Start by giving the model a curve.
level.w2-l8.hint2: A curve alone falls just short: raiders are rare, so the model is too shy to flag them. Lower the threshold, or give raider points more weight (then raise the threshold to match).
level.w2-l8.hint3: Degree 2 is enough for a round border; higher degrees chase the noise unless you regularize. Try degree 2, regularization 0.02, threshold 0.3.
level.w2-l8.debrief: You won the Boundary Plains. A curve for the shape, restraint against the noise, a fair say for the rare class, and a threshold chosen for the goal. F1 kept you honest: it is the harmonic mean of precision and recall, so it only rises when both do. These are the everyday decisions of real classification work.
concept.f1-score.definition: The harmonic mean of precision and recall: 2·P·R ÷ (P + R). It is high only when both are high, so it can't be gamed by flagging everyone or no one. The usual single score for a rare class.
level.boss.oversample.label: Weight of each raider point
level.boss.oversample.hint: ×1 = counts like anyone else. Higher values make a missed raider cost more in training.
level.boss.matrix.threshold: Flag as a raider when the model is at least this sure
level.boss.matrix.threshold.hint: Moves the border without retraining. 0.5 = the default.
level.result.boss.passed.title: The border holds
level.result.boss.failed.title: The border is breached
level.result.boss.failed.body: Hidden F1 {f1}; you need {target}. Precision {precision}%, recall {recall}%.
level.result.next.test_f1: Next star: a hidden F1 of at least {value}.
level.result.matrix.none.body: Nobody was invited, so no hill folk were found; you need {target}% of them.
level.result.boss.none.body: Hidden F1 {f1}: the border flagged no one, so every raider slipped through. You need {target}.
